vignette:
Captain Maya Chen is twenty-nine years old, a combat pilot who flies F-35s out of a joint base in the Pacific. She has been flying since she was twenty-three, logging over a thousand hours in theater. She came to talk because she can’t sleep, because her hands shake when she holds a coffee cup, because she has stopped talking to her mother on the phone.

It started eighteen months ago. Maya was scrambled on a night mission over hostile terrain, a routine CAS run. Her wingman, Captain Jake Morrison—ten years older, quiet, a man who always let her lead on the radio and bought her pad thai on R&R—was flying low cover. She saw the surface-to-air flash on her left peripheral, heard the garbled call over comms, then silence. She orbited for twenty minutes waiting for his beacon. It never came. The recovery team found nothing but sheet metal.

In the weeks after, Maya threw herself into sorties. She told herself the best way to honor him was to keep flying. She flew harder, lower, faster. Then the dreams started. In them, Jake is still alive, sitting in the ready room, and he turns to look at her, but his face is made of chrome and she can’t hear what he says. She wakes up with her sheets soaked, her heart pounding. She stopped drinking coffee because it made her jump at the smell of jet fuel.

She avoids the hangar now. She drives the long way to the flight line so she doesn’t pass the maintenance bay where Jake’s locker used to be. When she straps into the cockpit, her hands freeze on the throttle. She has to repeat the preflight checklist three times because her mind drifts to the radio silence, to the way the afterburner flame looked orange against the smoke. Her squadron commander noticed a drop in her simulator scores. He suggested she see someone.

Maya lives alone in a one-bedroom near base. She hasn’t dated since the incident. She says she doesn’t have the energy. She spends her nights cleaning her pistol, over and over, or watching old movies on mute. She rarely eats. She lost twelve pounds. She stopped replying to her mother’s texts—her mother lives in a city half a world away, and the last time they video-called, Maya started shaking and said the connection was bad. She feels a constant, low-grade guilt. She should have seen the SAM. She should have called a break turn sooner. If she had, maybe Jake would still be alive.

At work, she is functional but hollow. She can still fly—her muscle memory is intact—but the joy is gone. She feels like she is operating a machine that used to be her body. When the briefing officer says “hostile territory,” she sees Jake’s canopy shattering. When she hears a siren on base, she flinches. She has started checking the memorial page for the squadron every morning, even though she knows no one else has died. She doesn’t know why she does it.

The therapist notes that Maya’s narrative is precise, almost clinical. She uses aviation jargon to describe her feelings: “My affect is flat, like a dead-stick landing.” She doesn’t cry when she talks about Jake. She says she has already cried all she can. But at night, she lies awake, and she sees his wedding ring on his flight glove, and she hears the last transmission, just static.

She is a combat pilot. She was trained to never leave a wingman behind. But he is gone, and she is still flying, and that feels like the worst kind of betrayal.
